question: A Project Manager announces that, because the project now uses PM²-Agile, the team will stop using the standard PM² processes and artefacts. What does the PM²-Agile Guide say?

options.A: PM²-Agile replaces the PM² artefacts whenever software is delivered.
options.B: PM²-Agile replaces the PM² governance model with an Agile equivalent.
options.C: PM²-Agile does not replace any part of PM²; it expands the methodology.
options.D: PM²-Agile replaces the PM² phases for every team that works in sprints.

explanation: The guide states plainly that **PM²-Agile** does not replace any part of **PM²**. It expands PM² by providing specific methods, tools and techniques that help teams use Agile and Lean principles inside their PM² projects. That is why option C is correct. The strongest wrong answer is B: the PM² governance model, roles and artefacts stay in place, and PM²-Agile only adds to them.

question: According to the PM²-Agile Guide, PM²-Agile explains how to apply PM² to projects in which:

options.A: every team working on the project applies the same Agile practices.
options.B: at least one team of the Project Core Team applies Agile practices.
options.C: the supplier has been contracted to deliver the solution with Scrum.
options.D: the Project Steering Committee has formally approved an Agile pilot.

explanation: The guide says PM²-Agile explains how to apply PM² to projects where at least one team, part of the **Project Core Team (PCT)**, is applying Agile practices. One Agile team inside the project is enough. Option A is the common misreading: the guide never asks the whole project to be Agile before PM²-Agile can be used.

question: What does the guide give as the purpose of the Centre of Excellence in PM² (CoEPM²)?

options.A: To provide the Institutions with support, infrastructure and consulting.
options.B: To audit the European Commission projects for methodological compliance.
options.C: To certify all the project managers of the European Union Institutions.
options.D: To approve the Business Cases of all the inter-institutional projects.

explanation: The purpose of the **CoEPM²** is to provide the European Commission and the European Union Institutions with high-quality project management infrastructure, support and consulting services. It also supports the PM² Methodology internally, coordinates the **Project Support Network (PSN)** and promotes the wider adoption of PM². Option B is wrong because the guide gives the CoEPM² a support, consulting and coaching role, not a compliance-audit role.

question: How does the guide describe the PM² Project Support Network (PSN)?

options.A: A commercial network of the accredited PM² training and coaching firms.
options.B: An external network of the project management units of the Member States.
options.C: A standing board of senior project managers reporting to the Commission.
options.D: An internal network of Project Support Offices coordinated by the CoEPM².

explanation: The guide defines the **PSN** as an internal network of **Project Support Offices (PSOs)**, coordinated and supported by the **CoEPM²**. It shares knowledge, experience and best practices and collects feedback that is used to improve PM². Option B is the strongest distractor: the guide does describe a PSN outside the European Institutions, but the network itself is defined as a network of PSOs, not of Member State units.

question: The manager of a communication project asks whether the PM²-Agile Guide can be used outside software projects. What does the guide state?

options.A: It can be used only by software projects that are run by internal IT teams.
options.B: Most of its practices, tools and techniques can also be used on non-IT projects.
options.C: Non-IT projects must first turn their deliverables into software work items.
options.D: It can be used only by projects whose main deliverable is working software.

explanation: The guide says it primarily addresses the needs of software development projects, but it adds that Agile approaches are also frequently applied successfully outside software engineering. Therefore most of the practices, tools and techniques described in the guide can also be used on non-IT projects. Option D is the misconception being corrected here: "primarily" does not mean "only".

question: Which of the following does the guide list as a challenge faced by Agile implementors?

options.A: Applying Agile methods consistently across the whole organisation.
options.B: Finding certified Agile coaches for each of the project teams.
options.C: Convincing the suppliers to accept fixed-price delivery contracts.
options.D: Replacing the existing governance bodies with Agile equivalents.

explanation: The guide names two challenges: being Agile while complying with enterprise processes, structures and rules (IT governance, budgeting rules, programme structures, architecture and interoperability), and applying Agile methods consistently across the organisation. It warns that Agile may not be as effective if some teams work in an Agile way and others do not. Option D is wrong: the challenge is to be Agile while complying with the existing structures, not to remove them.

question: How does the guide define Agile at the start of the chapter 'About Agile'?

options.A: A contracting model that fixes the scope, the cost and the final deadline.
options.B: A set of software tools that automate the planning and the testing work.
options.C: An approach set out by principles and values, focused on valuable solutions.
options.D: A project lifecycle in which each phase is signed off before the next one.

explanation: The guide defines **Agile** as an approach described by a set of principles and values that focuses on delivering valuable solutions. It promotes adaptive planning, evolutionary development, early delivery, continuous improvement and a rapid, flexible response to change. Option B is the popular confusion: tools may support Agile, but the guide defines Agile by its values and principles, not by a toolset.

question: Which statement does the guide list among the key characteristics of Agile?

options.A: Scope is frozen at the start and changed only by formal requests.
options.B: Decisions are postponed until all of the requirements are known.
options.C: Plans are produced by planners and then handed over to the team.
options.D: Documentation and control are kept to just enough for the work.

explanation: The list of key characteristics ends with "just enough documentation and control". The same list includes delivering value early and frequently, decisions based on what is known, and scope management by continuous (re)prioritisation of the **Work Items**. Option B reverses the guide: decisions are based on what is known now, they are not delayed until everything is known.

question: According to the guide, what are the main principles of Lean?

options.A: The transparency of the value stream and the reduction of waste.
options.B: The stability of the team and the reduction of the project cost.
options.C: The automation of testing and the reduction of the release time.
options.D: The visibility of the backlog and the reduction of the team size.

explanation: The guide says Agile has been significantly influenced by the philosophy of **Lean**, whose main principles are the transparency of the value stream and the reduction of waste. Lean then identifies seven types of waste that Agile addresses in various ways. Option C names a real Agile practice, but automated testing is a technique, not one of the main principles of Lean.

question: Which item appears in the guide's list of the seven types of waste identified by Lean?

options.A: Rework – repeating the tasks that have already been accepted.
options.B: Escalation – raising the issues later than they should be raised.
options.C: Extra processing – steps in the process that are not really needed.
options.D: Over-commitment – accepting more work than the team is able to do.

explanation: The seven types of waste listed in the guide are inventory, overproduction, extra processing, transportation, waiting, motion and defects. Extra processing is described as additional steps in the process that are not really needed. Option A is attractive because rework sounds like waste, but the guide's term for flaws in the deliverables is "defects", and rework is not on the list.

question: A team asks how Agile deals with defects, the seventh type of waste. What does the guide answer?

options.A: Defects are reduced by adding a dedicated test phase before release.
options.B: Defects are reduced by building quality into the development process.
options.C: Defects are reduced by enlarging the acceptance test team at the end.
options.D: Defects are reduced by delaying delivery until every test has passed.

explanation: The guide says defects are reduced by ensuring quality in the development process, as opposed to investing in detection and correction activities. It names **Test-Driven Development** and pair programming as specific techniques that help to lower the defect rate. Option A is exactly the traditional answer the guide argues against: a test phase at the end is detection, not prevention.

question: What does the guide say about the Manifesto for Agile Software Development of 2001?

options.A: It defines twelve values that are supported by four core principles.
options.B: It defines seven values that are supported by seven core practices.
options.C: It defines four values and four supporting Agile team disciplines.
options.D: It defines four values that are supported by twelve principles.

explanation: In 2001 seventeen people brainstormed and produced the **Agile Manifesto**, which defines four values supported by 12 principles. The guide adds that this manifesto provides a foundation for the **PM²-Agile** framework. Option A simply swaps the two numbers, which is the classic trap on this point.

question: A developer says that "working solutions over comprehensive documentation" means documentation has no value at all. How does the guide describe the "X over Y" statements?

options.A: They define preferences, not alternatives; the right-hand side still counts.
options.B: They define alternatives, so the items on the right-hand side are dropped.
options.C: They define priorities that apply only to the software development teams.
options.D: They define strict rules which the Project Manager is not allowed to tailor.

explanation: The guide explains that you should value the concepts on the right-hand side, but value the things on the left-hand side even more. The manifesto defines preferences, not alternatives: it encourages a focus on certain areas without eliminating the others. Option B is precisely the misconception the guide corrects, so it cannot be the answer.

question: The guide adapts the Agile Manifesto for PM²-Agile. Which adaptation does it describe?

options.A: The focus moves from all stakeholders to the customers who pay for the work.
options.B: The focus moves from solution delivery back to software development work.
options.C: The focus moves from customers to all stakeholders, who are equally important.
options.D: The focus moves from the organisational ecosystem to the development team.

explanation: The guide lists three adaptations. The scope broadens from software development to solution delivery, the focus moves from customers to all stakeholders who are equally important, and the view widens from development teams to the overall organisational ecosystem. Option B reverses the first adaptation, so it contradicts the guide.

question: Why does PM²-Agile say "working solutions" where the original manifesto says "working software"?

options.A: Because the original manifesto authors changed the word in a later edition.
options.B: Because software is one part of an IT project and Agile also fits non-IT work.
options.C: Because a solution is always a document while software is a technical output.
options.D: Because the word software is not used for the European Commission projects.

explanation: The guide gives two reasons for preferring the word "solutions": to stress that software is only one part of an IT project, and to enable **PM²-Agile** to be applied to non-IT projects. Option C is wrong: the guide only says that on a non-IT project the core deliverable could be a document, not that a solution is always a document.

question: A supplier states that once the contract is signed there is no more need to talk to the stakeholders. What does the guide say about contracts?

options.A: Contracts remove the need for change management during the project.
options.B: Contracts are forbidden on Agile projects and should never be signed.
options.C: Contracts replace stakeholder collaboration once the scope is agreed.
options.D: Contracts bring a false sense of security; collaboration handles change.

explanation: The third Agile value is **stakeholder collaboration over contract negotiation**. The guide says contracts signed early lead to burdensome change management procedures and bring a false sense of security, while collaboration is what solves the issues and finds the opportunities not foreseen in the contract. Option B is too strong: the value is a preference, not a ban on contracts.

question: According to the fourth Agile value, how detailed should the plans of an Agile project be?

options.A: Every iteration of the project has to be planned in full detail up front.
options.B: Only the current iteration is detailed; longer-term plans stay high-level.
options.C: No plan is produced, because the team responds to change when it comes.
options.D: The release plan is detailed while the iteration plans are kept high-level.

explanation: The guide says it is very important to have a plan, but it should only be detailed for the current iteration. Longer-term planning is allowed, but those plans should be high-level and may need frequent updating. This value is described as the key enabler of the **Build-Measure-Learn** feedback loop from the **Lean Startup** model. Option C is wrong: responding to change never means working without a plan.

question: How does the guide describe Agile teams?

options.A: Self-organising, cross-functional, fluid and highly collaborative.
options.B: Cross-functional, permanent, co-located and led by a team manager.
options.C: Specialised, hierarchical, stable and supervised by the team leads.
options.D: Self-organising, single-skilled, fixed in size and fully outsourced.

explanation: The guide states that the most important productivity factor in any team is the people and the way they interact, and that Agile teams are self-organising, cross-functional, fluid and highly collaborative. "Fluid" means the team composition may vary over time. Option B is wrong on two points: the guide does not place a team manager over the team, and a permanent composition is the opposite of fluidity.

question: A team leader prepares the plan alone and then hands it to the team. What does the guide say about who should plan and organise the work?

options.A: The Project Manager plans the work and the team then executes the plan.
options.B: The team plans the work, but the estimates are set by the team leader.
options.C: The Business Manager plans the work with the Solution Provider only.
options.D: The people best-suited to plan the work are the ones who do the work.

explanation: The guide says the team is self-organising and that the people best-suited to plan and organise the work are the ones who do the work. It adds that this results in better estimates, more realistic schedules and increased commitment to the plan. Option B is close but still wrong: the team makes its own estimates, and that is exactly why the estimates improve.

question: The guide says a self-contained team should have the skills and knowledge to get the job done. What does it add for situations where this is not possible?

options.A: The missing work is outsourced to a separate supplier project team.
options.B: The work waits until the missing skill has been recruited into the team.
options.C: Outside experts may be brought in for brief periods for specific tasks.
options.D: The Project Manager performs the tasks that the team cannot perform.

explanation: The guide states that a self-contained team should have the skills and knowledge to get the job done, that this is not always possible, and that there is then a need to bring in outside experts for brief periods of time for specific tasks. Option A is wrong: passing the work to a separate team creates exactly the hand-offs (waste type 4) that Agile tries to remove.

question: A new team member asks what the difference is between a review and a retrospective. What does the guide state?

options.A: Reviews collect feedback about the solution; retrospectives about the process.
options.B: Reviews collect feedback about the process; retrospectives about the solution.
options.C: Reviews are held with the team while retrospectives are held with the users.
options.D: Reviews are held at the end of a project while retrospectives are monthly.

explanation: The guide describes reviews and retrospectives as rituals where teams learn from experience and plan changes for the next cycle. **Reviews** are a tool to collect feedback from the stakeholders and learn about the solution; **retrospectives** are a tool to collect feedback and learn about the process and the Agile team itself. Option B simply swaps the two, which is the trap in this item.

question: PM²-Agile treats Validated Learning as a cornerstone. Where does this concept come from?

options.A: From the Agile Manifesto, where it is one of the twelve principles.
options.B: From the Scrum framework, where it is part of the retrospective.
options.C: From the Project Support Network and its lessons learned database.
options.D: From the Lean Startup model, which is one of the pillars of PM²-Agile.

explanation: The guide says PM²-Agile embraces the concept of **Validated Learning**, which is a part of the **Lean Startup** model, and that this model plays an important role in PM²-Agile. Option C is wrong: the guide keeps the **Lessons Learned** captured at the end of a project as valuable, but that is a different practice from validated learning during the project.

question: In the Build-Measure-Learn loop, what does the team decide after analysing the data from the experiment?

options.A: Whether the release plan needs the approval of the Project Owner.
options.B: Whether the project may move on to the next management phase.
options.C: Whether the team should persevere with the idea or pivot it.
options.D: Whether the iteration should be extended to finish the backlog.

explanation: The guide describes the loop as turning ideas into products, measuring users' reactions and behaviours against the built products, and then deciding whether to persevere or pivot the idea; the process repeats as many times as necessary. The loop also emphasises speed, so the total time through the loop is minimised. Option B belongs to the PM² phase gates, not to the **Build-Measure-Learn** loop.

question: A team says its Minimum Viable Product is ready because the features work, although accessibility was skipped. What does the guide say?

options.A: Functionality is enough, provided the product reaches the users early.
options.B: All the key elements must be met, accessibility standards included.
options.C: Accessibility is added only after the users have accepted the MVP.
options.D: Design and usability replace accessibility in an early prototype.

explanation: The guide lists six key elements that an **MVP** must include: functionality, accessibility, reliability, design, usability and value. It says it is highly recommended to incorporate all of those elements instead of shortcutting and focusing on just one or two, and the first success criterion is to comply with all key elements. Option A is precisely the shortcut the guide warns against.

question: The guide lists "Agile is a silver bullet" among the Agile myths. How does it answer this myth?

options.A: Agile removes the project risks that come from changing priorities.
options.B: Agile projects cannot fail once the team becomes self-organising.
options.C: Agile guarantees the delivery of the solution within the budget.
options.D: You can fail as in any project, but with Agile you may fail sooner.

explanation: The guide answers that you can fail as in any other project, but with Agile you might fail sooner and, in doing so, you save resources. Agile is therefore not a guarantee of success. Option B is the myth itself stated in other words, which is exactly what the guide is correcting.

question: A team tells its Project Owner that Agile teams do not produce documentation. How does the guide answer this myth?

options.A: They do not produce documentation that is not necessary.
options.B: They produce documentation only after the final release.
options.C: They produce all documentation before the first iteration.
options.D: They replace documentation with automated testing reports.

explanation: The guide's answer to the myth "Agile teams do not do documentation" is short and clear: they do not produce unnecessary documentation. The second Agile value also reminds the reader that deliverable documentation, such as user manuals and operations manuals, is in fact part of the overall solution. Option D is wrong: test reports do not replace the documentation that belongs to the solution.

question: How does the guide answer the myth that Agile is anti-planning?

options.A: Planning happens only once, at the start, and is not repeated.
options.B: There is extensive planning on several levels, with high visibility.
options.C: Planning is replaced by the continuous reprioritisation of the work.
options.D: Planning is done by the Project Manager outside the iteration cycle.

explanation: The guide answers that in Agile development there is extensive planning on multiple levels, and with high visibility. Option C is the strongest distractor: continuous (re)prioritisation of the **Work Items** is how Agile manages scope, and it is added to planning rather than replacing it.

question: Which planning artefacts and events does the guide name when it refutes the anti-planning myth?

options.A: A Project Work Plan, a Gantt chart and the monthly steering meetings.
options.B: A Business Case, a Project Charter and the Project Handbook reviews.
options.C: A Release Plan, iteration plans and the daily Stand-up Meetings.
options.D: A Deliverables Acceptance Plan, a test plan and the weekly reports.

explanation: The guide states that there is a Release Plan, there are iteration plans, and daily work is planned during **Stand-up Meetings**. It adds that different tools support planning, for example the product and iteration backlogs. Option B lists genuine PM² artefacts, but they are not the ones the guide names when it answers this myth.

question: A manager claims that Agile is undisciplined because the team has no fixed process. What does the guide state?

options.A: Agile development trades discipline for a faster delivery to users.
options.B: Agile development leaves the choice of process to each developer.
options.C: Agile development is disciplined only when a supplier is involved.
options.D: Agile development is in fact extremely disciplined in its practices.

explanation: The guide answers this myth by saying that Agile development is, in fact, extremely disciplined. It names Continuous Integration, Automated Testing, iteration reviews and retrospectives, and iteration and release planning as examples of that discipline. Option A is wrong: speed in Agile comes from these disciplined practices, it does not come from dropping them.

question: Which statement does the guide use as evidence that Agile development is disciplined?

options.A: Every requirement is signed off before the development can start.
options.B: In most Agile practices all iterations and meetings are timeboxed.
options.C: The Project Manager approves each change made to the source code.
options.D: Each team follows the process defined by the quality assurance unit.

explanation: Under this myth the guide states that in most Agile practices all iterations and meetings are timeboxed, that there is a commitment to "ship product" regularly, and that improving the practice is part of the practice. Option D is wrong: the discipline described here comes from the team's own practices, not from a process imposed by another unit.

question: Which of the following is listed as an Agile myth in the PM²-Agile Guide?

options.A: Agile can only work when the whole team sits in the same room.
options.B: Agile removes the need for any supplier contract on a project.
options.C: Agile is anti-architecture and ignores the solution architecture.
options.D: Agile requires each team member to be a full-stack developer.

explanation: The guide lists six myths: Agile is a silver bullet, Agile teams do not do documentation, Agile is anti-planning, Agile is undisciplined, Agile is Scrum, and Agile is anti-architecture. Only option C appears on that list. Option B sounds plausible, because the third Agile value prefers **stakeholder collaboration over contract negotiation**, but the guide never presents it as a myth.

question: How does the guide answer the myth that Agile is Scrum?

options.A: Scrum is not the only Agile approach; there are at least ten more.
options.B: Scrum is the only Agile approach covering the whole project lifecycle.
options.C: Scrum is the Agile approach recommended for all PM²-Agile projects.
options.D: Scrum is an Agile approach that has never been very widely adopted.

explanation: The guide answers that Scrum is not the only Agile approach and that there are at least ten more. Option D contradicts the guide, which accepts as true that Scrum has become one of the most popular Agile frameworks. Being popular, however, does not make Scrum the only option or the recommended one.

question: A supplier proposes to manage the complete project lifecycle with Scrum alone. What does the guide state about Scrum?

options.A: Scrum covers the whole lifecycle once a Project Owner is appointed.
options.B: Scrum covers initiating and closing, but not the construction work.
options.C: Scrum covers the whole project lifecycle but not the construction.
options.D: Scrum focuses on construction and does not cover the whole lifecycle.

explanation: Under the myth "Agile is Scrum" the guide states that Scrum focuses mostly on the "construction" aspect of projects and that it does not address activities for managing the complete project lifecycle. This is one reason why **PM²-Agile** keeps the PM² lifecycle around the Agile work. Option C simply reverses the guide's statement.

question: Among the statements the guide makes about Scrum, which one is marked as true?

options.A: Scrum addresses the activities of the complete project lifecycle.
options.B: Scrum has become one of the most popular of the Agile frameworks.
options.C: Scrum is the only Agile approach used by the European Commission.
options.D: Scrum is the framework on which the whole PM²-Agile model is built.

explanation: In the myth "Agile is Scrum" the guide adds one statement followed by the word "(true)": Scrum has become one of the most popular Agile frameworks. Option A is explicitly denied on the same page, because the guide says Scrum does not address the activities for managing the complete project lifecycle.

question: An architect fears that the Agile team will simply ignore the solution architecture. What does the guide answer?

options.A: Solution architecture is valuable and is used in some way by Agile teams.
options.B: Solution architecture is produced in full before the first iteration.
options.C: Solution architecture is not needed, as it emerges from the code base.
options.D: Solution architecture is the responsibility of the Steering Committee.

explanation: The guide answers the myth "Agile is anti-architecture" by stating that solution architecture is valuable and that, in one way or another, it is used by Agile teams. It adds that solution architecture is minimised to what is known. Option C states the myth itself, so it is exactly what the guide corrects.

question: The PM²-Agile Guide states that PM²-Agile has adopted, with some modifications, the principles of the Agile Manifesto. How many PM²-Agile Principles are listed?
explanation: The guide prints **The 12 principles of PM²-Agile** and Appendix B.1 explains the same twelve one by one. The strongest trap is **17**: that is the number of authors of the **Agile Manifesto**, not the number of principles. **4** is the number of PM² phases and **10** is the number of **IAQs**.

question: PM²-Agile Principle 12 says that Agile practices should be enterprise-aware. Which three requirements does the principle name?

options.A: Fixed budgeting cycles, procurement and audit rules
options.B: Portfolio management, programme and operations rules
options.C: Information security, accessibility and usability rules
options.D: IT governance, enterprise architecture, interoperability

explanation: Principle 12 states that Agile practices should be **enterprise-aware** by considering **IT governance**, **enterprise architecture** and **interoperability** requirements. It adds that Agile teams should collaborate effectively with teams following alternative approaches. Portfolio, programme and IT operations are named elsewhere as neighbouring **Enterprise Practices**, not inside this principle, so that option is the strongest distractor.

question: How does the first PM²-Agile Principle state the highest priority?

options.A: To satisfy the client through early and continuous delivery of valuable solutions
options.B: To satisfy the customer through early and frequent delivery of working software
options.C: To satisfy the sponsor through early and predictable delivery of the agreed scope
options.D: To satisfy the users through complete and tested delivery of the final product

explanation: The exact wording is: the highest priority is to satisfy the **client** through early and continuous delivery of **valuable solutions**. The trap is the original Agile Manifesto wording, which says *customer* and *working software*. PM²-Agile deliberately changed both words, because the goal is a consumable **solution**, not only software.

question: According to the PM²-Agile Principles, what is the primary measure of progress?

options.A: The number of Work Items closed during each timeboxed iteration
options.B: The value and use of what has already been delivered
options.C: The share of planned documentation that has been completed
options.D: The earned value measured against the Project Work Plan

explanation: Principle 7 says the primary measure of progress is the **value and use** of what has been delivered; Appendix B.1 words the same principle as the **usefulness** of what has been delivered. **Earned value** is the strongest distractor, but Appendix B.1 explicitly rejects *some form of 'earned value' measure based on documentation's delivery or the holding of meetings*. Counting closed **Work Items** is activity, not delivered value.

question: PM²-Agile Principle 4 says that business people must work together throughout the project with which group?

options.A: The Project Steering Committee (PSC)
options.B: The Business Implementation Group (BIG)
options.C: The Project Support Team (PST)
options.D: The Project Core Team (PCT)

explanation: Principle 4 as printed in section 3.1 names the **Project Core Team (PCT)**. Appendix B.1 words it more loosely as *business people and project team*, but the team meant is the same one. The **BIG** is a business-side body that takes part in the **Iteration Review**; it is not the group named in this principle.

question: How do the PM²-Agile Principles define simplicity?

options.A: The art of reducing the size of the delivery team
options.B: The art of writing the smallest possible amount of code
options.C: The art of maximising the amount of work not done
options.D: The art of postponing decisions to the last moment

explanation: Principle 9 reads: *Simplicity – the art of maximising the amount of work not done – is essential.* It is about not doing low-value work at all, not about team size or code size. Postponing decisions to the last responsible moment is **Set Based Design**, a different idea in the guide, so that option is the strongest trap.

question: Appendix B.1 explains PM²-Agile Principle 3, 'Deliver value frequently through working solutions'. What iteration length does that explanation recommend?

options.A: Between one and two weeks, with a preference for the longer
options.B: Between two and four weeks, with a preference for the shorter
options.C: Between four and six weeks, with a preference for the shorter
options.D: Between three and six weeks, with a preference for the longer

explanation: Appendix B.1 states that Agile teams should deliver value at the end of each iteration and that iterations' length should be **between two and four weeks, with a preference for the shorter**. Note that the glossary gives a wider general range of one to four weeks; the question asks about the explanation of Principle 3, which is the tighter statement. Options with six weeks or a preference for longer iterations contradict the principle of frequent feedback.

question: A project team refuses every requirement change once the design has been signed off, in order to stop scope creep. How does Appendix B.1 describe processes of this kind?

options.A: They are change prevention processes, not change management processes
options.B: They are enterprise-aware controls demanded by the IT governance body
options.C: They are a valid tailoring choice recorded in the Development Handbook
options.D: They are sound baseline controls used by mature Agile delivery teams

explanation: Principle 2 says **changing requirements are welcome, even late in the solution delivery lifecycle**. Appendix B.1 states that traditional processes designed to prevent or limit scope creep *are in fact change prevention and not change management processes*. Calling this an enterprise-aware control is the strongest trap: **enterprise awareness** (Principle 12) is about IT governance and interoperability, not about blocking requirement changes.

question: Which of the following does the PM² Methodology provide, according to the PM²-Agile Guide?

options.A: A key set of Agile ceremonies
options.B: A set of Agile tools and techniques
options.C: A set of effective mindsets
options.D: A set of software coding standards

explanation: The guide lists five things that PM² provides: a project governance structure, process guidelines, artefact templates, guidelines for using the artefacts, and **a set of effective mindsets**. **Ceremonies** and **Agile Tools & Techniques** are on the next list, which says what PM²-Agile adds on top of PM². PM² never provides coding standards, because it does not prescribe processes at the technical level.

question: Which item appears in the list of what PM²-Agile provides?

options.A: A project governance structure for the organisation
options.B: Artefact templates for all PM² management artefacts
options.C: Guidelines for using the four PM² lifecycle phases
options.D: Roles & Responsibilities extending the PM² Governance

explanation: PM²-Agile provides **Roles & Responsibilities (as an extension to the PM² Governance)**, integration with the PM² project lifecycle, **Core Themes**, a key set of **Ceremonies**, suggested **Agile artefacts**, an Agile glossary and Agile Tools & Techniques. The other three options are taken from the PM² list on the previous page. The word *extension* is the signal: PM²-Agile adds to PM² governance, it does not create a governance structure of its own.

question: Why does the guide say that the PM² approach enables the rapid adoption of Agile practices?

options.A: Because it prescribes Agile ceremonies for every project type
options.B: Because it does not prescribe processes at the technical level
options.C: Because it removes governance constraints from delivery teams
options.D: Because it replaces the phase lifecycle with timeboxed cycles

explanation: The guide says PM² *has built-in flexibility and does not prescribe specific processes at the technical level*, and that this approach enables the rapid adoption of Agile practices. Removing governance is the opposite of the guide's message: Agile teams are expected to **fully account for higher-level governance constraints by aligning with PM²**. PM² keeps its serial phase lifecycle, so replacing it is also wrong.

question: The guide lists organisational factors that IT projects must consider. Which one is on that list?

options.A: A traditional command and control management culture
options.B: A fully outsourced software development delivery model
options.C: A continuous, unconstrained annual investment budget
options.D: A strong matrix organisation with dedicated project staff

explanation: The listed factors are a fixed budgeting cycle, a traditional command and control management culture, a traditional waterfall project lifecycle, a functional/weak matrix project organisation, a clear project-approval milestone, and upfront planning and architecture decisions. Two options are inversions of that list: the guide names a **fixed** budgeting cycle, not an unconstrained one, and a **functional/weak** matrix, not a strong matrix. Outsourcing is not in the list at all.

question: A team proposes to abandon the PM² phases and manage the project with a purely Agile approach. What position does the guide take?

options.A: It is acceptable once the Business Case has been formally approved
options.B: It is the preferred option whenever the solution is a software system
options.C: It is possible only for small teams working in small organisations
options.D: It cannot fully satisfy certain project management requirements

explanation: The guide states that PM² acknowledges the positive contribution of the Agile attitude, *however, certain management requirements cannot be fully satisfied by using a purely Agile project management approach*. PM² therefore keeps a governance structure with a **serial phase lifecycle** while endorsing an enterprise-aware Agile approach. The small-organisation option is the strongest trap: the guide contrasts small and large organisations, but it never says a purely Agile approach replaces PM² for small teams.

question: How does the guide describe what PM²-Agile is?

options.A: A new Agile philosophy designed for the European Commission
options.B: A replacement for the PM² project governance structure
options.C: A software engineering library of development practices
options.D: A tailoring of proven Agile and Lean practices linked to PM²

explanation: The guide says plainly: *PM²-Agile is not a new Agile philosophy or approach. PM²-Agile simply tailors proven Agile and Lean practices and connects them to PM².* The 'new philosophy' option is the direct negation of that sentence, so it is the strongest trap. PM²-Agile keeps the PM² governance model rather than replacing it.

question: What does the guide say about PM²-Agile and software engineering?

options.A: It is not a software engineering library, but includes optional techniques
options.B: It is a software engineering library that prescribes development practices
options.C: It excludes all software engineering techniques from its published scope
options.D: It replaces software engineering practices with a set of Agile ceremonies

explanation: The guide states that *though PM²-Agile is not a software engineering library, it does include some optional techniques such as Test-Driven Development, Pairing, etc.* It adds that PM²-Agile is well-integrated with software engineering practices because it is used primarily for software development. The 'excludes all techniques' option is the strongest distractor, because it takes the first half of the sentence and ignores the second half.

question: According to the guide, how does PM² support the Agile idea of self-organising teams?

options.A: It limits self-organisation to the Agile Team Members alone
options.B: It hands self-organisation decisions to the IT governance body
options.C: It gives a governance framework that lets the PCT self-organise
options.D: It replaces self-organisation with a command and control culture

explanation: The guide says Agile advocates self-organising teams and that PM² *provides the appropriate governance framework, which reflects the governance needs of the organisation as a whole, but also enables the **Project Core Teams (PCT)** to harness the benefits of self-organisation*. A traditional **command and control** culture is listed on page 14 as an organisational constraint to deal with, not as something PM² imposes, so that option is the strongest trap.

question: According to the PM²-Agile Guide, how many distinct phases does a PM² project pass through?

options.A: Three
options.B: Four
options.C: Five
options.D: Six

explanation: The guide states that *projects pass through four distinct phases, as described by PM²*: **Initiating**, **Planning**, **Executing** and **Closing**. This stays true when Agile is used, because PM²-Agile adds iterative cycles inside the phases rather than removing the phases. Choosing three or five usually comes from confusing phases with the three levels of iterative cycles.

question: What does the PM²-Agile 'CIR' rhythm stand for?

options.A: Clarify, Improve, Report
options.B: Commit, Iterate, Retrospect
options.C: Coordinate, Implement, Review
options.D: Collaborate, Integrate, Release

explanation: The **CIR rhythm** is **Coordinate, Implement, Review**. The guide says that all cycles follow this rhythm regardless of their duration, so it applies to daily cycles, iterations and releases alike. The other options mix Scrum-flavoured vocabulary that the guide does not use for CIR.

question: PM²-Agile has iterative cycles at three levels. Which three?

options.A: Daily cycles, iterations and releases
options.B: Iterations, releases and project phases
options.C: Daily cycles, sprints and increments
options.D: Ceremonies, iterations and milestones

explanation: The guide states that PM²-Agile has iterative cycles at three levels: **daily cycles**, **iterations** and **releases**. Project phases are not one of the three levels; they are the serial PM² frame inside which the cycles run, which makes that option the strongest trap. The word *sprint* is Scrum vocabulary and is not used here.

question: What does the guide say about the order of work at project level and at team level?

options.A: Both the project phases and the team-level tasks follow a strict order
options.B: The team tasks are sequential while the project phases fully overlap
options.C: Neither the project phases nor the team-level tasks are in any order
options.D: The project is sequential, but team tasks are not, within iterations

explanation: The guide says the overall sequential character follows the concept that a project has a defined start and end, so activities must start with initiating and planning, then implementation, then acceptance, transitioning and closing. It then says *team-level tasks do not have a sequential character within iterations: planning, analysing, coding, testing and reviewing are done in every iteration*. Option B reverses the two levels, which is the classic mistake.

question: What does the guide say about the interfaces between the project phases?

options.A: They are fixed by the Product Owner in the Release Plan
options.B: They disappear completely when an Agile approach is used
options.C: They are seldom clearly separated, so activities continue
options.D: They are marked by formal gates that stop earlier activities

explanation: The guide states that *the interfaces between phases are seldomly separated clearly* and that activities of one phase, such as planning, continue during the following phases. The guide is explicit that project phases still exist under Agile and that a common understanding of them should be fostered, so 'they disappear' is wrong. A hard gate that stops earlier activities contradicts the overlapping shown in the lifecycle figures.

question: Early in a PM²-Agile project there is much uncertainty about the solution. What does the guide say the team should do about its assumptions?

options.A: Convert them into approved facts so that planning can proceed
options.B: Identify and declare them, so they can be questioned and tested
options.C: Send them to the IT governance body for review and sign-off
options.D: Store them in the Deployment Plan for the Transition Iteration

explanation: At the start of the project the concern is to understand what to build, and PM²-Agile *acknowledges the need to identify and declare all the assumptions*. The guide says that declaring assumptions and **not treating them as facts** gives stakeholders and the team the chance to ask questions and discuss the problem. Hypotheses are then identified and tested to validate the assumptions and reduce uncertainty risk early.

question: A PM²-Agile project is nearing completion. According to the guide, where should the focus shift?

options.A: To integrating the solution and preparing organisational ownership
options.B: To adding the remaining low-priority Work Items to the last iteration
options.C: To shortening the iterations so that more value can still be delivered
options.D: To rewriting the Business Case so it matches the delivered solution

explanation: The guide says that as the project nears completion the focus shifts to ensuring the solution is well-integrated into the overall project deliverables and contributes to the benefits the organisation wants. It also emphasises that the organisation must be able to assume ownership and accountability for the evolution and maintenance of the system when the project closes. Filling the last iteration with low-priority items contradicts the rule that every iteration takes the highest-priority Work Items.

question: How does the guide define an Agile iteration?

options.A: A meeting where the team plans the work for the coming weeks
options.B: A period in which the team documents the agreed requirements
options.C: A phase of the PM² lifecycle assigned to the Agile team members
options.D: A period in which the A-PCT produces a potentially shippable part

explanation: An **iteration** is defined as a period of time within a project in which the **Agile Project Core Team (A-PCT)** produces a stable, **potentially shippable** part of the solution, together with any necessary supporting documentation or deliverables. The strongest trap is calling it a phase: an iteration sits inside the PM² phases, it is not one of them. An iteration is a period of work, not a meeting.

question: Iterations in PM²-Agile are timeboxed. What does the guide say this means?

options.A: The scope is fixed and the duration is adjusted to fit the scope
options.B: The duration is fixed and the scope of the content is managed
options.C: Both the duration and the scope are fixed before the work starts
options.D: The duration is agreed with the client at the end of each cycle

explanation: The guide says iterations are timeboxed, *meaning the iteration duration is fixed, and the scope of the iteration's content is actively managed to meet that schedule*. Option A reverses this: fixing scope and moving the date is exactly what timeboxing avoids. Fixing both duration and scope removes the flexibility that lets the team meet the schedule.

question: Each iteration must dedicate part of its time to lay the foundation for the following iteration. Which element plays this role?

options.A: The Iteration Review, a part of the Transition Iteration
options.B: The Definition of Done, a part of the Iteration Planning
options.C: Design Blocks, a part of the Release Planning ceremony
options.D: The Work Items List, a part of the Development Handbook

explanation: The guide says this is where **Design Blocks (a part of the Release Planning ceremony)** play an important role, letting teams challenge the requirements received from the **Product Owner (PrOw)** and other business stakeholders. Inside Design Blocks, **Agile Team Members (ATeMs)** run workshops on low fidelity prototypes, and high fidelity prototypes follow for validation. The **Iteration Review** looks backwards at completed work, so it is not the element that prepares the next iteration.

question: PM²-Agile considers three ways of exposing work. Which set is correct?

options.A: Exposure of Work Items, end of an Iteration, and Release
options.B: Daily builds, the Iteration Review, and the Retrospective
options.C: Prototypes, Design Blocks, and the Deployment Plan review
options.D: Work Items, the Transition Iteration, and Project Reports

explanation: The three ways of exposing work are **exposure of Work Items**, **exposure at the end of an Iteration** (which supports the Iteration Review ceremony), and a **Release**. The guide notes that the goals are similar in all three, but the cadence and the required formalism differ. Daily builds and retrospectives exist in PM²-Agile, but they are not on this list of three, which makes that option the strongest trap.

question: A team is choosing what to put into its next iteration. What does the guide say each iteration should do?

options.A: Deliver every Work Item that the Product Owner has written
options.B: Implement the highest-priority items and the critical risks
options.C: Split the work evenly between features and technical debt
options.D: Keep the riskiest items until the integration test is finished

explanation: The guide says each iteration should implement the **highest-priority Work Items** and address the **most critical risks**, so that every iteration adds maximum value while reducing uncertainty. Postponing risky items is the opposite advice: the guide warns that discovering all problems late, in one massive integration, is what brings large projects down. The **Work Items List** is prioritised by the **Product Owner (PrOw)**, but not all of it fits in one iteration.

question: What happens at the beginning of each iteration in PM²-Agile?

options.A: The Project Manager approves the Development Work Plan
options.B: The Business Manager signs off the Definition of Done
options.C: The IT governance body validates the mandatory artefacts
options.D: The A-PCT commits to a goal agreed with the Product Owner

explanation: The guide states that at the beginning of each iteration the **Agile Project Core Team (A-PCT)** commits to a goal agreed with the **Product Owner (PrOw)**. That goal guides the team through the set of **Work Items** taken from the **Work Items List (WIL)**. The **Business Manager (BM)** takes part in the Iteration Review at the end of the iteration, not in setting the goal at the start.

question: Most Work Items were already exposed and informally validated during the iteration. What does the guide still require at the Iteration Review?

options.A: The review can be skipped because the feedback is already collected
options.B: Only the Work Items that were not exposed earlier must be reviewed
options.C: A formal check of each Work Item against the Definition of Done
options.D: A written approval from the IT governance body before the release

explanation: The guide says the **Iteration Review** is a prescribed event that requires a certain degree of formalism, and that *though much of the iteration content was previously exposed and validated with some degree of confidence, a formal check for each Work Item must be performed*. The check is against the team's **Definition of Done**. Continuous exposure makes the review better, but it never replaces it, so skipping or partial review is wrong.

question: How does the guide define a Release?

options.A: An agreed Solution Increment delivered to the client and users
options.B: The output shown to the Product Owner at each Iteration Review
options.C: A stable build produced by the continuous integration process
options.D: The set of Work Items completed during a single timeboxed cycle

explanation: A **Release** is *an agreed Solution Increment, delivered to the client and users so that they can start using it as a real product*, and it includes all the **Done** Work Items from several prior iterations. That last part is the key difference from an iteration: one iteration produces a potentially shippable increment, while a release gathers the output of several iterations for real use. A continuous integration build is a technical output, not a Release.

question: A team must train users and fix a critical defect before deployment. Where does the guide say this effort may be planned?

options.A: In the Closing phase, after the last iteration has been reviewed
options.B: In a separate project run by the Business Implementation Group
options.C: In the Release Planning ceremony held before the first iteration
options.D: In an iteration called a Transition Iteration, before the release

explanation: The guide says the extra preparation needed for a release, such as training users or fixing a critical bug, *may be planned as part of an iteration called a **Transition Iteration***. Its main purpose is to ensure a successful deployment of the solution into the production environment. Typical activities also include documenting the system, extra testing and updating the Development Plan or Deployment Plan.

question: A team is preparing a Transition Iteration. How should it be planned, according to the guide?

options.A: With a lighter process, since no new features are developed
options.B: Just like a regular iteration, with the proper ceremonies
options.C: As a phase of the PM² lifecycle, with a formal phase gate
options.D: Without a Work Items List, because the scope is already known

explanation: The guide is explicit: *a Transition Iteration has some different activities, but it doesn't mean that it is planned differently. It remains an iteration and as such, it should be carried out just like a regular one (proper ceremonies, Iteration Planning with a Work Items List, etc.)*. Different content does not mean a lighter process, which makes option A the strongest trap. The guide also notes that one Transition Iteration may not be enough.

question: The PM² Mindsets aim to integrate and complement the four pillars of PM². Which are they?

options.A: Governance, Ceremonies, Processes and Artefacts
options.B: Governance, Lifecycle, Ceremonies and Artefacts
options.C: Governance, Lifecycle, Processes and Artefacts
options.D: Governance, Lifecycle, Processes and Ceremonies

explanation: The guide names the four pillars of PM² as **Governance**, **Lifecycle**, **Processes** and **Artefacts**. **Ceremonies** are part of what PM²-Agile adds on top of PM²; they are not a PM² pillar, so every option containing them is wrong. The Mindsets sit alongside the pillars as reminders of effective attitudes and behaviours.

question: How many PM² Mindsets does the guide list?

options.A: Ten
options.B: Twelve
options.C: Three
options.D: Eleven

explanation: The guide presents **eleven PM² Mindsets** as eleven statements for Project Managers and project teams. **Ten** is the number of **IAQs** (Infrequently Asked Questions) printed on the next page, and it is the strongest trap. **Twelve** is the number of PM²-Agile Principles and of the PM²-Agile **Drivers**, and **three** is the number of main PM²-Agile mindsets.

question: The main mindsets of an Agile delivery approach in PM²-Agile focus on three things. Which set is correct?

options.A: Solution delivery, all project stakeholders, and the ecosystem
options.B: Software development, paying customers, and development teams
options.C: Working software, the client, and the self-organising Agile team
options.D: Value delivery, the Product Owner, and the Project Core Team

explanation: The three main PM²-Agile mindsets are focus on **solution delivery**, focus on **all project stakeholders**, and focus on the **overall organisational ecosystem and its improvement**. Option B is the strongest trap because it lists exactly what the guide says the original Agile Manifesto focused on – software development, 'customers', and development teams – and which PM²-Agile deliberately widened.

question: A Project Manager asks how PM²-Agile combines a serial project lifecycle with iterative delivery. Which PM²-Agile driver states this?

options.A: Organise work around timeboxes, not the other way around
options.B: Be serial in the large, and iterative in the small
options.C: Speak Agile, but also speak 'organisation'
options.D: Be as Agile as needed and as Agile as possible

explanation: **Be serial in the large, and iterative in the small** is the PM²-Agile driver that describes exactly this combination: PM² phases run in sequence at project level, while the team works iteratively inside them. The other three options are also genuine drivers, which is what makes this item hard, but they answer different questions. 'Speak Agile, but also speak organisation' is about **enterprise awareness** in communication, not about the lifecycle shape.

question: What does the guide say about the relationship between the PM² Mindsets and Agile?

options.A: They must be replaced by the PM²-Agile drivers on Agile projects
options.B: They apply only to the directing and managing layers of a project
options.C: They are fully aligned with the spirit of Agile and are extended
options.D: They conflict with Agile and are therefore tailored out by teams

explanation: The guide states that the PM² Mindsets are *100 % aligned with the spirit of Agile as presented in PM²-Agile* and that they are *further extended* by the PM²-Agile mindsets. The key word is **extended**: nothing is replaced or removed. That makes the 'replaced by the drivers' option the strongest trap.

question: What is the guide's position on documentation in PM²-Agile?

options.A: Agile does not mean no documentation, but rather just enough
options.B: Agile means that documentation is replaced by working software
options.C: Agile requires the same documentation set as any other project
options.D: Agile leaves all documentation decisions to the Product Owner

explanation: The guide says *Agile does not mean 'no documentation', but rather just enough*, and that 'enough' is defined by the needs of the project **and** by the corporate requirements for transparency, traceability and control. It adds that documentation must be **enterprise-aware** and aligned with PM² documentation requirements. 'Replaced by working software' is the popular misreading of Agile that this sentence exists to correct.

question: The PM²-Agile artefacts are grouped into three categories. Which set is correct?

options.A: Governance, Planning, and Monitoring & Control artefacts
options.B: Business, Development, and Operational Model artefacts
options.C: Mandatory, Recommended, and Optional project artefacts
options.D: IT Governance, Agile specific, and Coordination & Reporting

explanation: The three categories are **IT Governance Artefacts**, **Agile (development) Specific Artefacts**, and **Coordination & Reporting Artefacts**. IT Governance artefacts are common to all IT projects whatever the management approach; Coordination & Reporting artefacts give the Project Manager visibility of the **A-PCT** work. Mandatory/recommended/optional is a real PM² idea for artefacts, but it is not how PM²-Agile groups them here.

question: Which document is mandatory for projects that include information systems as part of the solution?

options.A: The Development Handbook that documents the tailoring
options.B: The Architecture Overview required by the IT Governance
options.C: The Deployment Plan used for the Transition Iteration
options.D: The Development Status Report sent to the Project Manager

explanation: The guide names four documents as mandatory under IT Governance: the **Business Case**, the **Project Charter**, the **Architecture Overview** and the **Operational Model**. The Development Handbook, Deployment Plan and Development Status Report are all supporting artefacts of PM²-Agile, but they are not on the mandatory list. The guide adds that an organisation's IT Governance may request further artefacts on top of these four.

question: A Project Manager asks where the team's Development Handbook belongs in the overall project documentation. What does the guide say?

options.A: It becomes a part of the overall Project Handbook
options.B: It replaces the Project Handbook on Agile projects
options.C: It is filed as an annex to the approved Business Case
options.D: It is kept only inside the Agile team and not shared

explanation: In the artefact list the guide writes *Development Handbook (becomes part of the overall Project Handbook)*, in the same way that the **Development Work Plan** becomes part of the **Project Work Plan** and the **Development Status Report** becomes part of the **Project Reports**. Keeping it inside the Agile team contradicts the aim of documenting Agile work to increase transparency between the directing, managing and performing layers.

question: What does tailoring mean in PM²-Agile?

options.A: Adding new Agile ceremonies to the published methodology guide
options.B: Selecting the Agile tools and techniques for a single iteration
options.C: Changing parts such as process steps, artefact contents or roles
options.D: Producing a new version of the guide for the whole organisation

explanation: The guide defines **tailoring** as *changing specific parts of the methodology, such as process steps, artefacts contents or the distribution of responsibilities amongst the various roles*. Organisations tailor in order to fit their structure, culture, processes and policies. The guide also warns that PM²-Agile *should not be seen as a one-size-fits-all approach* and should evolve as the team learns through each iteration, release or project.

question: Which artefact documents how and why PM²-Agile has been tailored for a project?

options.A: The Project Charter approved by the appropriate body
options.B: The Business Case that justifies the chosen solution
options.C: The Development Work Plan with the release schedule
options.D: The Development Handbook kept by the project team

explanation: The guide states that *the **Development Handbook** documents and describes how and why PM²-Agile has been tailored for a particular project*. It typically records the rationale for tailoring and deviations, variations from standard practice, tailoring of Roles & Responsibilities, the tools and formats used for each artefact, and the responsibilities for review and approval in a RASCI table. The Business Case justifies the project, not the tailoring choices.

question: An organisation wants one adapted version of PM²-Agile used by every project in a single department. Does the guide allow this?

options.A: No, tailoring is always decided by the Product Owner alone
options.B: Yes, tailoring can be done at division or department level
options.C: No, tailoring is only ever done for one individual project
options.D: Yes, but only if the IT governance body writes the guide

explanation: The guide says tailoring *can be also carried out at other levels like a Division, a department or even a smaller sector, and applied to all its projects*. So tailoring is not limited to a single project, which kills the strongest distractor. Project-level tailoring still happens as well, and it is recorded in the **Development Handbook**; the tailoring activity list ends with *review and agree on the tailoring*.

question: The PM²-Agile Guide lists three ways in which the Lean start-up model supports the Lean UX process. Which of the following is one of them?

options.A: Shifting mindsets from assumption to experimentation
options.B: Shifting decision rights from the team to the Project Owner
options.C: Shifting the test effort to the end of each iteration
options.D: Shifting architecture work to the Enterprise Architecture Office

explanation: The guide says the Lean start-up model supports **Lean UX** through three things: removing development waste with UX design, harmonising the relationships between the **Agile Project Core Team (A-PCT)** and the rest of the stakeholders, and shifting mindsets from assumption to experimentation. A repeats the third one. C is the strongest distractor, but moving testing to the end of an iteration is exactly what the **Concurrent Testing** practice of the Testing theme forbids.

question: In the Lean UX theme, how does the PM²-Agile Guide describe requirements before development starts?

options.A: As fixed commitments that must be signed off by the IT Governance body
options.B: As detailed specifications that must be complete before the Initiating phase
options.C: As assumptions that the Agile Project Core Team must validate before developing
options.D: As enabler items that must be estimated in points during the Executing phase

explanation: **Lean UX** focuses on the principle that requirements are assumptions which the **Agile Project Core Team (A-PCT)** needs to validate before it starts developing. Because development costs time and effort, rapid prototypes create the learning that lets the team move forward. B is the strongest distractor: complete upfront specifications are the traditional approach that the guide contrasts with Agile, not the Lean UX view.

question: In the third step of the PM²-Agile Lean UX process the prototyped experience is deployed. What does the guide say this act of deploying means?

options.A: It always requires a release into the production infrastructure
options.B: It freezes an experiment so it can serve as a validated learning tool
options.C: It hands the prototype over to the IT operations team for support
options.D: It closes the iteration and triggers the Iteration Retrospective event

explanation: The step **Deploy a Prototype** follows the agreement between the business stakeholders and the **A-PCT**. The guide states clearly that the act of deploying does not necessarily imply a technical deployment: the goal is to freeze an experiment that is ready for the next step and can be used as a validated learning tool. A is the strongest distractor because the word deploy suggests production, but the guide explicitly denies this.

question: PM²-Agile comments on the Agile core value 'Responding to change over following a plan'. What does the guide conclude about the planning effort?

options.A: Planning effort is replaced by daily coordination inside the iterations
options.B: Planning effort is concentrated in the Initiating phase of the project
options.C: Planning effort is smaller because plans are thrown away every iteration
options.D: Planning effort is greater than it is in traditionally managed projects

explanation: The guide notes that the Agile value refers to following a plan, and not to planning. It then states that the amount of planning effort in Agile involves more effort in comparison to traditionally managed projects. C is the strongest distractor because the guide does say 'do the planning, throw away the Plan', but that phrase is about the value of plans, not about reducing the effort.

question: Managing and Directing stakeholders on a PM²-Agile project ask for a complete plan with a definite budget before the project starts. What does the Planning theme advise?

options.A: Freeze the Work Items List so that the budget can be fixed early
options.B: Involve and educate them in transparent Agile planning and tracking
options.C: Move the detailed planning of every iteration to the Initiating phase
options.D: Delegate the plan to the Architecture Owner and the Business Manager

explanation: The guide recognises that Managing and Directing stakeholders usually prefer to receive complete plans before the project starts. It advises involving and educating these stakeholders in transparent Agile planning and progress tracking, so that the efficacy of the Agile process can be demonstrated. A is the strongest distractor, but PM²-Agile keeps the **Work Items List (WIL)** open and re-prioritised, and measures work with iterations, story points and velocity instead.

question: Which statement is one of the principles for planning that PM²-Agile promotes?

options.A: Planning is more important than plans: do the planning, throw away the Plan
options.B: Plans are more important than planning: keep the Plan, repeat the planning
options.C: Planning belongs to the Project Manager: the team executes the agreed Plan
options.D: Planning is done once per release: the Plan is then frozen until delivery

explanation: PM²-Agile promotes three planning principles: the planning cycles and scope are decided per the cycle they belong to and the nature of the project, everybody is involved in planning, and planning is more important than plans. C is the strongest distractor because a Project Manager does exist in PM², but the guide states the opposite: everybody is involved in planning.

question: Which of the following is listed as a theme for coordination between the Agile Project Core Team (A-PCT) and other groups of stakeholders?

options.A: Recruitment of the Agile Team Members for the next release
options.B: Procurement of development tools from external vendors
options.C: Architecture artefacts following organisation standards
options.D: Training of end users during the Business Implementation

explanation: The guide names five coordination themes: Planning, Reporting, **Architecture**, Deployment and Transition, and Risk. For architecture it says the artefacts should be created following organisation standards, so that impact assessment, reusability and interoperability analysis can be done without extra overhead. D is the strongest distractor because user training is a real PM² concern, but it is not one of the five listed coordination themes.

question: A Team Coordinator (TeCo) asks which events carry the external coordination between the A-PCT and the other project layers and stakeholders. Which set does the guide give?

options.A: Daily Stand-up, Iteration Planning and Iteration Review
options.B: Iteration Review, Iteration Retrospective and Daily Stand-up
options.C: Release Planning, Iteration Planning and Iteration Review
options.D: Project follow-up meetings, Project Status Reports and Demos

explanation: External coordination is facilitated through regular project meetings and reports. The guide lists the external communication events as project follow-up meetings, **Project Status Reports**, and demos and deliverables acceptance events. A and B are strong distractors because the **Daily Stand-up**, **Iteration Planning**, **Iteration Review** and **Iteration Retrospective** are listed separately as internal coordination ceremonies inside the A-PCT.

question: PM²-Agile says there should be three main groups of reporting and planning units. To which group does a user story belong?

options.A: Work units, together with enabler stories and bugs
options.B: Functional units, together with features and use cases
options.C: Delivery units, together with work packages and deliveries
options.D: Business units, together with capabilities and processes

explanation: The three groups are delivery units (for example work packages and deliveries), functional units (for example use cases, business processes, capabilities and features) and work units (work items such as user stories, enabler stories and bugs). A user story is a work unit. B is the strongest distractor: features are the functional unit one level above, and the guide asks you to group the smaller stories into a feature and to link a group of features to a delivery.

question: Which two levels of abstraction does PM²-Agile acknowledge as key for describing the behaviour of a solution?

options.A: Epics and Features, described in the PM² Business Case
options.B: Features and Stories, described from high to low detail
options.C: Themes and Epics, described in the Development Workplan
options.D: Use Cases and Test Cases, described in the Project Charter

explanation: Under the dimension **Abstraction Level**, the guide states that PM²-Agile acknowledges the key role of **Features** and **Stories** to describe the solution's behaviour. A and C are the strongest distractors because 'epic' and 'theme' are common Agile words, but the PM²-Agile Guide never uses an epic level. Features are described at a high level in the **Project Charter** and are then decomposed into stories.

question: To ensure proper requirements management, implementation and monitoring, PM²-Agile considers two dimensions. Which pair does the guide name?

options.A: Business Value and the Size of each work item
options.B: Risk Likelihood and Risk Impact of each item
options.C: Delivery Units and the Functional Units of work
options.D: Abstraction Level and Implementation Perspective

explanation: The guide names two very important dimensions to describe a solution's behaviour: **Abstraction Level**, which gives Features and Stories, and **Implementation Perspective**, which gives Business and Enabler items. A is the strongest distractor because **Business Value** and 'Size' are real PM²-Agile terms, but they are the recommended criteria for prioritising features, not the two requirement dimensions.

question: A Work Items List contains almost only business items, and the team now struggles to deliver because the architecture is weak. Who does the guide say should help the Product Owner (PrOw) restore the balance?

options.A: The Business Manager (BM), who owns the feature priorities
options.B: The Team Coordinator (TeCo), who protects the team capacity
options.C: The Architecture Owner (ArOw), who balances enabler work
options.D: The Project Owner (PO), who approves the Architecture Overview

explanation: The guide states that the **Architecture Owner (ArOw)** plays a very important role in helping the **Product Owner (PrOw)** find the right balance between business and enabler work. Focusing only on business items gives good initial results, but velocity drops when the lack of a solid architecture becomes obvious. A is the strongest distractor: the **Business Manager (BM)** does take part in prioritising features, but the guide gives the balancing role to the ArOw.

question: In PM²-Agile, which of the following belongs to Enablement Work?

options.A: Writing the user acceptance criteria for a business feature
options.B: Evaluating options and preparing the legal compliance work
options.C: Prioritising the Work Items List with the Business Manager
options.D: Demonstrating the increment to users at the Iteration Review

explanation: **Enablement Work** is the non-business effort that makes the business features possible. The guide says it includes architecture, infrastructure, evaluating options, legal compliance, continuous improvement and other non-functional requirements. A feature with this perspective is an **Enabler Feature** and a story with it is an **Enabler Story**. A is the strongest distractor, because acceptance criteria are attached to business work as well and are not in the enablement list.

question: PM²-Agile estimation is based on three main concepts. Which of the following is one of them?

options.A: Absolute Estimate, translating points into an estimate of effort
options.B: Earned Value, translating points into a cost performance index
options.C: Function Points, translating features into a normalised size
options.D: Critical Path, translating stories into a scheduled duration

explanation: The three concepts are **Relative Estimate**, **Velocity** and **Absolute Estimate**. The Absolute Estimate translates the size of a work item, measured in points, into an objective and detailed estimate of effort, typically in actual hours. B is the strongest distractor because earned value sounds like project control, but the guide does not use it in this theme.

question: A team prioritises its Work Items List with the MoSCoW technique. Which split of the total effort does the guide mention as suggested by some methodologies?

options.A: 80% Must have, 10% Should have and 10% Could have
options.B: 50% Must have, 30% Should have and 20% Could have
options.C: 40% Must have, 40% Should have and 20% Could have
options.D: 60% Must have, 20% Should have and 20% Could have

explanation: The guide states that some methodologies suggest assigning 60% of the total effort to 'Must have' requirements, 20% to 'Should have' and 20% to 'Could have'. Contingency is then applied by still delivering the 'Must have' items when the other work cannot be finished in time. A is the strongest distractor, but an 80% share for 'Must have' would leave almost no contingency, which defeats the purpose of **MoSCoW**.

question: Which statement about Relative Estimates matches the PM²-Agile Guide?

options.A: They convert points into actual hours for each work item
options.B: They become less reliable as the project moves forward
options.C: They tend to be more accurate as the project progresses
options.D: They are produced by the Project Owner before the release

explanation: A **Relative Estimate** gives a high-level estimate of the size of a work item, usually in a neutral unit such as points, and rests on the fact that people are better at estimating relatively. The guide says relative estimates tend to be more accurate as the project progresses, because the problem and the solution become clearer. A is the strongest distractor: converting points into actual hours is the definition of the **Absolute Estimate**.

question: PM²-Agile describes two types of risk management approach. What does the guide mean by the implicit approach?

options.A: Risk management comes out naturally from the iterative planning and review
options.B: Risk management is delegated to the Project Manager outside the iterations
options.C: Risk management uses risk-based spikes and risk Boards inside iterations
options.D: Risk management is limited to a quantitative analysis of the PM² Risk Log

explanation: The guide defines **Implicit** risk management as what is intrinsic to the Agile process, where risk management comes out naturally from the iterative planning and review activities. **Explicit** risk management means applying specific tools and techniques to identify, assess and mitigate risk. C is the strongest distractor, because risk-based spikes and risk Boards are named by the guide as tools of the explicit approach.

question: The Risks theme names three Agile Manifesto principles that make PM²-Agile less risky by nature. Which of the following is one of them?

options.A: Fixed scope, so that the release content never changes
options.B: Simplicity, maximising the amount of work not done
options.C: Documentation, so that every decision is traceable
options.D: Contract negotiation, so that liabilities are shared

explanation: The three principles given are collocated teams, **Simplicity** and regular reflection. Simplicity means maximising the amount of work not done: the team concentrates on the minimum work needed, and removing waste is itself a risk management practice. C is the strongest distractor, but the Agile Manifesto values working software over comprehensive documentation, and the guide does not list documentation here.
