C is the strongest distractor because both artefacts talk about delivery, but the Operational Model is about infrastructure, not about release timing.

question: A small Agile Project Core Team asks whether the Development Handbook must be kept as a document separate from the Project Handbook. What does the guide say?

options.A: It must always be produced and archived as a separate document
options.B: It replaces the Project Handbook once PM²-Agile is being used
options.C: It does not have to be a separate information carrier of its own
options.D: It is only needed when several teams work on the same project

explanation: The guide says the **Development Handbook** is identified as a separate artefact but does not have to be a separate information carrier; depending on the project's nature there might be a single container for both artefacts, even with synchronised configuration management. B is the strongest distractor: the Development Handbook is an extension of the **Project Handbook** and must stay aligned with it, so it never replaces it.

question: An Iteration Retrospective produces an agreed change to the team's way of working. Where does the guide say such changes should be documented?

options.A: In the Development Work Plan of the Agile Project Core Team
options.B: In the Development Handbook, because it is a living document
options.C: In the Development Status Report sent to the Project Manager
options.D: In the Iteration Plan of the iteration that has just finished

explanation: The guide states that the **Development Handbook** is a living document and that any changes or improvements suggested as the outcome of ceremonies such as **Iteration Retrospectives** or **Iteration Reviews** should be documented there. A is the strongest distractor: the **Development Work Plan** is also a living artefact, but it holds the work itself - the **Work Items List**, **Release Plan** and iterations - not the way of working.

question: Which three elements does the Development Work Plan contain?

options.A: The Business Case, the Project Charter and the Release Plan
options.B: The Work Items List, the Test Plan and the Deployment Plan
options.C: The Project Work Plan, the Release Plan and the Iterations
options.D: The Work Items List, the Release Plan and the Iterations

explanation: The **Development Work Plan** is a container of different perspectives on what has to be done. It includes the **Work Items List (WIL)**, the corresponding **Release Plan** and the supporting iterations, and these three elements let the **Agile Project Core Team (A-PCT)** manage the expectations of the other members of the project organisation. B is the strongest distractor: the **Test Plan** and the **Deployment Plan** are separate Agile-specific artefacts.

question: The Development Work Plan becomes part of which PM² core artefact?

options.A: The Project Work Plan
options.B: The Project Handbook
options.C: The Project Charter
options.D: The Project Status Report

explanation: The guide says the **Development Work Plan** becomes part of the **Project Work Plan** and therefore should be aligned with the important project milestones defined by the **Project Manager (PM)** and the whole **Project Core Team (PCT)**. B is the strongest distractor: it is the **Development Handbook** that becomes part of the **Project Handbook**. The **Development Status Report** is the artefact that feeds the **Project Status Report**.

question: The Development Work Plan has two levels of schedule detail. What is the focus of each level?

options.A: The Release Plan focuses on how, the Iteration Plan on what and when
options.B: Both plans focus on which team member will perform each single task
options.C: The Release Plan focuses on what and when, the Iteration Plan on how
options.D: The Release Plan focuses on cost, the Iteration Plan on quality levels

explanation: The guide describes two schedule detail levels: a release level schedule (**Release Plan**) and an iteration level schedule (**Iteration Plan**). In the Release Plan the focus is primarily on what needs to be done and when; in an Iteration Plan the focus is on how the **Agile Project Core Team (A-PCT)** will do it. A is the strongest distractor because it simply inverts the two focuses.

question: The Agile Project Core Team asks who is responsible for which part of the Development Work Plan. According to the key participants table, which answer is correct?

options.A: The TeCo for the Work Items List, the PrOw for the Release Plan
options.B: The PrOw for the Work Items List, the TeCo for the Release Plan
options.C: The PM for the Work Items List, the TeCo for the Release Plan
options.D: The PrOw for the Work Items List, the ArOw for the Release Plan

explanation: The **Team Coordinator (TeCo)** is responsible for collecting the data of all activities in the **Development Work Plan** in general and for the **Release Plan** in particular. The **Product Owner (PrOw)** is responsible for the **Work Items List (WIL)** and is an important contributor to the release and iteration plans. A is the strongest distractor because it swaps the two roles. The **Project Manager (PM)** is accountable, not responsible.

question: Which items are typically included in the Work Items List (WIL)?

options.A: Defects, enabler stories and user stories to be built
options.B: Risks, issues and change requests raised by the team
options.C: Milestones, deliverables and the phases of the project
options.D: Test cases, releases and the planned iteration goals

explanation: The guide lists defects (or bugs), **enabler stories** and **user stories** as the items typically included in the **Work Items List (WIL)**. All of them are prioritised, effort-estimated and tracked in terms of progress. B is the strongest distractor: risks, issues and changes live in the **project logs**, although managing those logs can generate new work items that are then added to the WIL.

question: How does the PM²-Agile Guide describe a Work Item?

options.A: A contract between the team and the Product Owner
options.B: A signed acceptance record for a delivered feature
options.C: A complete technical specification of one component
options.D: A pointer to something that needs to be implemented

explanation: The guide is explicit: a **Work Item** is not a contract between the development team and the **Product Owner (PrOw)** but rather a pointer to something that needs to be implemented. A is therefore the strongest distractor, because it states exactly what the guide denies. Each Work Item commonly refers to further information such as business rules, diagrams or user interface specifications, which is why it is not a complete specification either.

question: A team wants to start its first iteration, but the Work Items List is clearly not complete. What does the guide advise?

options.A: Wait until every single work item has been written and estimated
options.B: Start only after the governance body approves the short list
options.C: Start anyway, provided that the Work Items List is prioritised
options.D: Start with enabler stories until the business items are ready

explanation: The guideline 'Start working with a prioritised **Work Items List (WIL)**' says the list does not have to be complete for the **Agile Project Core Team (A-PCT)** to start working, but it must be prioritised. Without a prioritised WIL the team risks investing resources in items that are not so important. A is the strongest distractor: waiting for a complete list contradicts the agile approach the guide describes.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for the Work Items List, which responsibility does the Business Manager (BM) have?

options.A: Responsible
options.B: Supports
options.C: Consulted
options.D: Informed

explanation: The **Work Items List** row reads BM = S, PM = A, TeCo = C, PrOw = R, ArOw = S, ATeM = S. The **Business Manager (BM)** therefore **Supports**: as the representative of the **Project Owner** in daily project life, he gives inputs on business priorities, objectives and user needs. D is the strongest distractor because in most other Agile-specific artefact rows, such as the **Development Handbook** and the **Release Plan**, the BM is only **Informed**.

question: What is a main purpose of the Release Plan in PM²-Agile?

options.A: To record the daily work done by each Agile Team Member
options.B: To define the criteria used to assess the test results
options.C: To list all the tasks needed to build one single work item
options.D: To plan the release of usable versions of the solution

explanation: The guide lists the main purposes of the **Release Plan**, and the first one is to plan the release of usable versions of the solution. It also gives a high-level plan with the main goals and major features, offers visibility of risks and dependencies, and helps schedule transition and business implementation activities. C is the strongest distractor: decomposing work items into tasks belongs to the **Iteration Plan**, not to the Release Plan.

question: During a project the Work Items List has grown and the team's velocity has fallen. According to the guide, which two elements are used to evaluate the Release Plan's feasibility?

options.A: The size of the Work Items List and the team's velocity
options.B: The budget consumed and the number of open issues
options.C: The number of planned releases and of the iterations
options.D: The test coverage and the number of defects found

explanation: The guideline 'Release Plan Feasibility' says that new facts, data and decisions constantly affect the size of the **Work Items List (WIL)** and the team's velocity, and that these two elements evaluate the **Release Plan**'s feasibility, allowing business stakeholders to make adjustments. The guide adds that different data sets can create optimistic and pessimistic velocity scenarios. B is the strongest distractor: budget and issues are tracked at project level, but they are not the two feasibility elements named here.

question: An Iteration Planning ceremony is about to start. According to the guide, who defines the Iteration Goal and who commits to it?

options.A: The TeCo defines the goal and the Product Owner commits to it
options.B: The PM defines the goal and the Team Coordinator commits to it
options.C: The PrOw defines the goal and the Agile Project Core Team commits
options.D: The ArOw defines the goal and the Product Owner commits to it

explanation: The **Iteration Plan** includes the iteration start and end dates, the **Iteration Goal** defined by the **Product Owner (PrOw)** and committed to by the **Agile Project Core Team (A-PCT)**, and the list of work items needed to reach that goal. A is the strongest distractor: the **Team Coordinator (TeCo)** is responsible for developing the Iteration Plan, but the goal itself comes from the PrOw.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for the Iteration Plan, what is the responsibility of the Product Owner (PrOw)?

options.A: Responsible
options.B: Accountable
options.C: Supports
options.D: Consulted

explanation: The **Iteration Plan** row reads BM = I, PM = A, TeCo = R, PrOw = C, ArOw = S, ATeM = S. The **Product Owner (PrOw)** is **Consulted** by the **Team Coordinator (TeCo)** to provide the iteration goal and a prioritised **Work Items List (WIL)**, the main input for the plan. C is the strongest distractor: in the **Release Plan** and **Development Work Plan** rows the PrOw is marked **Supports**, but for the Iteration Plan the guide prints C.

question: The Agile Project Core Team must produce the Test Plan. Which role does the guide make responsible for drafting it?

options.A: The Team Coordinator (TeCo)
options.B: The Agile Team Member (ATeM)
options.C: The Architecture Owner (ArOw)
options.D: The Independent Tester (QA)

explanation: In the key participants table for the **Test Plan**, the **Agile Team Member (ATeM)** is responsible for drafting it and for giving technical advice on the testing activities, the scope and type of testing and the techniques used. A is the strongest distractor: the **Team Coordinator (TeCo)** only supports the drafting and ensures alignment with the **Project Handbook**. The **Project Manager (PM)** is accountable for how the team addresses testing.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for the Test Plan, what is the responsibility of the Team Coordinator (TeCo)?

options.A: Supports
options.B: Responsible
options.C: Accountable
options.D: Consulted

explanation: The **Test Plan** row reads BM = I, PM = A, TeCo = S, PrOw = S, ArOw = S, ATeM = R. The **Test Plan** is the one Agile-specific artefact where the **Agile Team Members (ATeM)** are **Responsible**, so the **Team Coordinator (TeCo)** only **Supports**. B is the strongest distractor because the TeCo is **Responsible** in most other rows, such as the **Development Handbook**, the **Release Plan** and the **Deployment Plan**.

question: A project must prepare its Deployment Plan. According to the guide's key participants, who is responsible for creating it?

options.A: The Architecture Owner (ArOw), who owns the technical decisions
options.B: The Agile Team Member (ATeM), who knows the delivery pipeline
options.C: The Team Coordinator (TeCo), working closely with the PM
options.D: The operational unit representative, who runs the platform

explanation: The **Team Coordinator (TeCo)** is responsible for creating the **Deployment Plan**, aligned with the **Development Work Plan** (release schedule) and with the project-level **Transition Plan**, in close collaboration with the **Project Manager (PM)**. D is the strongest distractor: the guide does list a representative of the relevant operational unit as a key participant, but that person only contributes information on operational processes and infrastructure and checks feasibility.

question: Which PM² artefacts complement the Deployment Plan by covering the strategy that makes the client organisation ready to use the system?

options.A: The Project Charter and the Communications Management Plan
options.B: The Quality Management Plan and the Risk Management Plan
options.C: The Project Work Plan and the Deliverables Acceptance Plan
options.D: The Transition Plan and the Business Implementation Plan

explanation: The guide says the PM² **Transition Plan** and **Business Implementation Plan** complement the **Deployment Plan** by covering the strategy that ensures the client organisation is ready to use the system, through training, support and similar activities. The Deployment Plan itself focuses on the technical side: cut-over, rollbacks and back-out procedures. C is the strongest distractor: the **Deliverables Acceptance Plan** deals with accepting deliverables, not with readiness of the client organisation.

question: How often can the Development Status Report be produced in a PM²-Agile project?

options.A: Only once at the end of each phase of the project
options.B: It can follow each iteration and/or each release
options.C: Every single week, as fixed by the PM²-Agile Guide
options.D: Only when the Project Manager formally asks for it

explanation: The guide says the **Development Status Report** can follow each iteration and/or each release, depending on the reporting needs defined for the project. Like the **Project Status Report**, it tracks cost, schedule, scope, risks, issues, changes and forecasts, and it is incorporated at the project reporting level. C is the strongest distractor: the guide fixes no weekly rhythm, it ties the report to the iteration and release cycle.

question: What is the difference between the release burndown chart and the iteration burndown chart?

options.A: The release chart tracks functionality, the iteration chart effort
options.B: The release chart tracks effort in hours, the iteration features
options.C: Both charts track the remaining effort, in story points or hours
options.D: The release chart tracks defects, the iteration chart the velocity

explanation: The guide states that, unlike the iteration burndown chart which tracks remaining effort in points or hours, the release burndown chart tracks functionality, to see whether the team is delivering working software in each iteration. B is the strongest distractor because it inverts the two charts. The release chart is reviewed at least once each iteration; the iteration chart is the primary tool for understanding the status of the current iteration.

question: How often should the iteration burndown chart be updated?

options.A: Once at the end of each iteration, during the review
options.B: Frequently, and preferably every day of the iteration
options.C: Only when the Project Manager requests a status report
options.D: Once per release, just before the Release Planning starts

explanation: The guide says the iteration burndown chart should be updated frequently, preferably daily, because daily or frequent updates allow the team to react to changes. Such reactions can include removing work items from the iteration or from the **Work Items List**, lowering the ambition of an item, or finding better ways to approach the work. A is the strongest distractor: updating only at the **Iteration Review** would come far too late to let the team react.

question: In the RAM (RASCI) for the Development Status Report, what is the responsibility of the Architecture Owner (ArOw)?

options.A: Responsible
options.B: Supports
options.C: Consulted
options.D: Informed

explanation: The **Development Status Report** row reads BM = I, PM = A, TeCo = R, PrOw = I, ArOw = I, ATeM = S. The **Architecture Owner (ArOw)** is therefore only **Informed**. B is the strongest distractor: the **Agile Team Members (ATeM)** are the ones who **Support** the report, by providing information on the work they perform daily, while the **Team Coordinator (TeCo)** prepares it and the **Project Manager (PM)** is accountable.

question: In the PM²-Agile table of project logs, the Retrospectives Log refers to which PM² artefact?

options.A: The Project Status Report
options.B: The Project Handbook
options.C: The Project-End Report
options.D: The Quality Review Report

explanation: The table in section 7.3.2 maps each item to its PM² reference: risks to the **Risk Management Plan** and **Risk Log**, issues to the **Issue Log**, decisions to the **Decision Log**, changes to the **Change Log**, the **Testing Log** to the **Test Plans** and **Deliverables Acceptance Plan**, and the **Retrospectives Log** to the **Project-End Report**. A is the strongest distractor: progress information does flow into status reporting, but the guide prints the Project-End Report for the Retrospectives Log.

question: A multi-annual project follows PM²-Agile. How does the guide describe the use of the Project Progress Report on such a project?

options.A: More frequently than usual, for example bi-monthly or quarterly
options.B: Once a year only, exactly as in any standard PM² project
options.C: Once at the end, since the Development Status Report replaces it
options.D: Only at each phase gate, when the governance body meets

explanation: For projects that follow **PM²-Agile**, the **Project Progress Report** is a frequent reporting tool, for example bi-monthly or quarterly, as opposed to yearly for multi-annual projects. The higher frequency lets the **Project Core Team (PCT)** capture and manage significant scope changes. B is the strongest distractor: yearly reporting is exactly the standard practice that PM²-Agile changes. The report still gives a high-level overview of the whole project and its actual status.

question: A new Agile team keeps missing its commitments and avoids difficult conversations. The Team Coordinator (TeCo) proposes the **Assessing Teamwork** technique. Which five key fundamentals does that assessment cover?

options.A: Vision, trust, autonomy, discipline and fast delivery
options.B: Respect, courage, openness, focus and full commitment
options.C: Trust, conflict, commitment, accountability and results
options.D: Trust, communication, conflict, velocity and results

explanation: The guide bases **Assessing Teamwork** on Patrick Lencioni's *The Five Dysfunctions of a Team*. It names exactly five key fundamentals of a cohesive and productive team: trust, conflict, commitment, accountability, and results. Option B is the strongest distractor because those are the five Scrum values, which the PM²-Agile guide does not use here. Options A and D mix real words with invented ones such as autonomy and velocity.

question: A department head wants **Self-Organising Teams** in her area. According to the PM²-Agile guide, what must managers do to make this work?

options.A: Create the conditions that let teams thrive and keep self-organising
options.B: Specify in advance the effective behaviours that the teams must follow
options.C: Run a single set-up workshop that establishes self-organisation for good
options.D: Delegate the whole decision to the Team Coordinator (TeCo) of each team

explanation: The guide says managers must create the conditions that enable teams to thrive and continue to self-organize. It adds that they must guide the behaviours that emerge, instead of specifying in advance what effective behaviour is, which kills option B directly. Option C is the strongest trap, but the guide states that **Self-Organising** is a process and not something that is done once and for all. Promoting self-organising teams is described as a strategic decision needing effort at many organisational levels, so it cannot be delegated to one role.

question: A UX specialist is asked to take part in a **Design Blocks** session for the next iteration. What is that person's role during the workshop?

options.A: To write the acceptance criteria for every work item in the iteration
options.B: To approve the Architecture Overview before any coding work starts
options.C: To decide the priority order of the features in the Work Items List
options.D: To facilitate and coordinate the team while it sketches a prototype

explanation: In **Design Blocks** the facilitator and coordinator is the UX specialist. That person drives all participants to prepare a low fidelity prototype by sketching the future feature together, and makes sure design, interaction, behaviour, requirements and technical matters are discussed and agreed. Option C is the strongest distractor, but prioritising the **Work Items List** belongs to the Product Owner (PrOw), not to the UX specialist.

question: In **Design Blocks**, what happens once the Agile Project Core Team (A-PCT) feels confident about the low-fidelity version of a feature?

options.A: The Product Owner (PrOw) adds the feature to the Release Plan baseline
options.B: The User Interface (UI) designers produce a high-fidelity prototype
options.C: The Agile Team Members (ATeMs) start writing the acceptance test cases
options.D: The Architecture Owner (ArOw) signs off the Architecture Overview draft

explanation: The guide describes a two-step sequence for **Design Blocks**. First the team builds a low-fidelity prototype together; then the User Interface (UI) designers provide a high-fidelity prototype in which UI standards from existing design libraries are applied. That high-fidelity prototype then drives the coding of the feature as part of the team's daily work. Option C is the strongest distractor because coding does follow, but the guide places the high-fidelity prototype between the sketch and the code.

question: How does the PM²-Agile guide distinguish a **Feature** from a **Story**?

options.A: A feature is estimated in hours; a story is estimated in relative points
options.B: A feature is a defect report; a story is a request for new functionality
options.C: A feature is written by the client; a story is written by the team members
options.D: A feature is a service the solution gives; a story is a vertical slice

explanation: The guide states that **Features** represent services or functionalities delivered by a solution to tackle the stakeholders' needs, while **Stories** are small pieces corresponding to vertical slices of the system's desired functionality. The difference is one of size and scope, not of author or of estimation unit. Option A is the strongest distractor because relative estimation is indeed used in PM²-Agile, but the guide does not define features and stories by their estimation unit.

question: The guide says a feature is very unlikely to be implemented within one iteration's scope. What reason does it give?

options.A: Because every feature must first be approved by the governance body
options.B: Because features are estimated in ideal days, which iterations exclude
options.C: Because a feature includes all relevant scenarios, so it is lengthy
options.D: Because the Work Items List accepts only items sized under one iteration

explanation: The guide says implementing a feature is a more complex and lengthy process than implementing a story, because a feature includes all relevant scenarios. That is why every feature has to be decomposed into its corresponding stories before they enter the **Work Items List (WIL)**. Option D is the strongest distractor: it sounds like a sensible rule, but the guide gives the reason as the feature's own breadth of scenarios, not as a rule of the **Work Items List**.

question: The guide lists four benefits of **User Stories Breakdown**. Which statement describes the benefit it calls Reduced Variability?

options.A: Smaller stories improve design, raising maintainability and scalability
options.B: Smaller stories travel faster through the system and shorten the queue
options.C: Smaller stories are simpler to describe, so they reduce uncertainty
options.D: Smaller stories mean smaller changes, which are easier to incorporate

explanation: For Reduced Variability the guide says that smaller stories are simpler, have less variability, often do not delay delivery, and travel faster through the implementation process, reducing the length of queues. The other three options are the guide's own other three benefits of **User Stories Breakdown**, which makes them strong distractors. Option C is Risk Reduction, option A is Modular Implementation, and option D is Easier response to change.

question: In PM²-Agile, what does an agreed **Definition of Done** (DoD) apply to, and who checks it?

options.A: A release, checked by the Project Steering Committee (PSC)
options.B: An iteration goal, checked by the Product Owner (PrOw)
options.C: A project phase, checked by the Project Manager (PM)
options.D: A Work Item, checked by the Agile Team Members (ATeMs)

explanation: The guide defines the **Definition of Done** as the conditions that must be satisfied for a given **Work Item** to be considered complete. It is a set of items that the **Agile Team Members (ATeMs)** check to decide whether an implemented Work Item meets the team's quality standards. Option B is the strongest distractor because the Product Owner does accept work, but the guide attaches the DoD to the Work Item and to the ATeMs, not to the iteration goal.

question: Two Agile teams inside the same organisation disagree about what done means. What does the PM²-Agile guide say about this situation?

options.A: The Project Manager (PM) must impose one Definition of Done on both teams
options.B: Each team must keep its own Definition of Done private to avoid conflict
options.C: A common Definition of Done may be applied by different development teams
options.D: The Definition of Done is fixed in the Development Handbook and is frozen

explanation: The guide says that in some organisations a common definition of done may be available and can be applied by different development teams, moving towards a cross-project understanding of what done means. The **Definition of Done** should still result from the development team's own discussion and agreement. Option A is the strongest distractor: a shared DoD is allowed, but the guide never gives the **Project Manager (PM)** the power to impose it on the teams.

question: How does the PM²-Agile guide describe **Planning Poker**?

options.A: A consensus-based technique for relatively estimating the size of goals
options.B: A time-boxed technique for sequencing the tasks on the critical path
options.C: A voting technique for choosing which release to deploy to production
options.D: A prioritisation technique for ordering the Work Items List (WIL) items

explanation: The guide defines **Planning Poker** as a consensus-based technique for relatively estimating the size of the development goals. It is an efficient way of reaching agreement without spending too much time, and it lets team members express their opinions and concerns. Option D is the strongest distractor because it confuses estimation with prioritisation; prioritising the **Work Items List** is a separate activity owned by the Product Owner (PrOw).

question: According to the guide, what does the word Kanban mean, and where was it first used?

options.A: Card in Japanese, first used in Lean manufacturing at Ford Motor Company
options.B: Flow in Japanese, first used inside the Toyota software engineering library
options.C: Signal in Japanese, first used in Japanese post-war shipbuilding yards
options.D: Board in Japanese, first used in Toyota's Production System for cars

explanation: The guide says Kanban means Board in Japanese and is an essential tool used in visual management. It was first used in Toyota's Production System for cars, letting upstream operations produce a part only when downstream operations required it. Option A is the strongest distractor because Card is the common translation quoted outside PM², and Ford is often named as the origin of mass production, but the **Kanban Method** section names Toyota.

question: A team's board shows large amounts of half-finished work waiting between stages. Which method does the guide associate with this build-up of inventory waste?

options.A: The pull method, where the last step tells the previous step it is ready
options.B: The push method, where inventory waste builds up at chain bottlenecks
options.C: The Design Blocks method, where assumptions are challenged before coding
options.D: The burndown method, where the planned work is burnt down towards zero

explanation: The guide says that in traditional push methods, inventory waste is built up during the production process as bottlenecks are experienced in the production chain. In the pull method used by the **Kanban Method**, the last step tells the previous step when it is ready to produce, and this pull is passed back step by step to the first step. Option A is the strongest distractor because it describes the pull method correctly, but pull is the cure for the build-up, not its cause.

question: What does a **Burndown Chart** plot when it tracks the progress of a release, rather than the progress of an iteration?

options.A: Story points across iterations, not effort hours across days
options.B: Effort hours across days, not story points across iterations
options.C: Defects found across releases, not story points across days
options.D: Story points across days, not effort hours across iterations

explanation: The guide gives two cases. **Burndown Charts** track the progress of iterations using effort hours or story points across days, and the progress of releases using story points across iterations. Option B is the strongest distractor because it states the iteration case correctly, but the question asks about the release case. Option D swaps the two units and the two time scales.

question: The guide states that **Burndown Charts** are dynamic. What does it mean by that word?

options.A: The chart is redrawn automatically by the continuous integration tool
options.B: The vertical axis rescales itself whenever the team's velocity changes
options.C: The planned work may change from feedback received during development
options.D: The chart shows the iteration and the release trend in one single picture

explanation: The guide says **Burndown Charts** are dynamic in the sense that the planned work may change as a result of the feedback received during development. Dynamic therefore refers to the changing plan, not to the drawing technology. Option A is the strongest distractor because automation is common in practice, but the guide makes no such claim. The guide's other two statements are that these charts should be highly visible and that they highlight obstacles hindering the team's performance.

question: What is the correct order of steps inside one **Test-Driven Development** cycle, as the guide describes it?

options.A: Write implementation code, then a test, then run the test to see it pass
options.B: Write a small test, run it to confirm it fails, then write just enough code
options.C: Write the full test suite, then all the code, then run every test one time
options.D: Write acceptance criteria, then a test, then hand the code to a tester

explanation: The guide says the developer first writes a small test to validate a piece of code, then runs the test to confirm that it fails as a sanity check, and only then writes just enough implementation code to make that test pass. In each cycle the tests come first. Option A is the strongest distractor because it is the normal test-after habit that **Test-Driven Development** replaces.

question: How long does the guide say one **Test-Driven Development** cycle usually lasts?

options.A: It is bounded by the length of the daily stand-up meeting
options.B: It runs for one full iteration, so two to four weeks
options.C: It matches one working day of the developer involved
options.D: It is short and rarely goes beyond ten minutes in total

explanation: The guide states plainly that the **Test-Driven Development** cycle is short and rarely goes beyond 10 minutes. This very short loop is what lets developers take small steps when writing software, which the guide calls safer and far more productive than writing code in large increments. Option B is the strongest distractor because two to four weeks is the guide's iteration length, not the TDD cycle length.

question: PM²-Agile distinguishes **Pairing** from **Pair Programming**. Which statement matches the guide?

options.A: Pairing covers activities such as design or testing; Pair Programming is the coding case
options.B: Pairing is done by two Team Coordinators; Pair Programming is done by two Agile Team Members
options.C: Pairing is a coaching relationship; Pair Programming is strictly between two peer developers
options.D: Pairing happens within an iteration; Pair Programming happens only in Design Blocks sessions

explanation: The guide defines **Pairing** as two **Agile Team Members (ATeMs)** working together on a particular activity, such as designing a subset of the solution, coding, or testing. When the activity is programming a piece of the system, the technique is known as **Pair Programming**. Option C is the strongest distractor because the guide says the opposite: Pair Programming does not assume a coaching relationship, since both developers are peers.

question: A manager wants to run **Pair Programming** as the official training scheme, always pairing a junior with a senior developer. What does the guide say?

options.A: Pair Programming does not assume a coaching relationship; the two are peers
options.B: Pair Programming is designed as the organisation's on-the-job training method
options.C: Pair Programming must always pair a senior developer with a junior developer
options.D: Pair Programming replaces code review, so no other quality check is needed

explanation: The guide is explicit that **Pair Programming** does not assume a coaching or training relationship, because both developers are peers working on the same project. It only adds that if a pair happens to include a senior and a junior, some degree of on-the-job training will naturally take place. Option B is the strongest distractor because it turns that side effect into the purpose. The guide's stated value of pairing is instant and real-time work review, which raises deliverable quality.

question: Under PM²-Agile principle 3, Deliver value frequently through working solutions, how long should an iteration be?

options.A: Between four and six weeks, with a preference for the longer one
options.B: Exactly four weeks, so that reporting aligns with the month end
options.C: Between one and two weeks, and never longer than a fortnight
options.D: Between two and four weeks, with a preference for the shorter

explanation: Appendix B.1 states that Agile teams should deliver value at the end of each iteration, and that iterations' length should be between two and four weeks, with a preference for the shorter. Frequent delivery gives business stakeholders the chance to give timely feedback. Option C is the strongest distractor, since shorter is preferred, but two weeks is the floor the principle sets. Note that the **Glossary** entry for Iteration gives a wider range of one to four weeks as the most commonly used durations.

question: Appendix B.1 criticises the change management processes that traditional project teams often adopt. What does it call them?

options.A: Risk avoidance processes that move scope decisions to the client
options.B: Change prevention processes, not change management processes
options.C: Governance processes that protect the baseline set in the charter
options.D: Scope creep processes that let requirements grow without control

explanation: Principle 2 of the **PM²-Agile Principles** says traditional teams often adopt change management processes designed to prevent or limit scope creep, and that these are in fact change prevention and not change management processes. The Agile alternative is to develop functionality in a well-established priority order and to let requirements evolve as stakeholders understand their needs better. Option D is the strongest distractor because it reverses the point: the guide criticises the processes for blocking change, not for allowing uncontrolled growth.

question: In Appendix B.1, what is the primary measure of progress, and which measure is explicitly rejected?

options.A: The usefulness of what has been delivered; earned value is rejected
options.B: The number of closed work items; a burndown-based measure is rejected
options.C: The team's velocity per iteration; a client satisfaction survey is rejected
options.D: The percentage of budget spent; a documentation-based count is rejected

explanation: Principle 7 of the **PM²-Agile Principles** in Appendix B.1 reads: the primary measure of progress is the usefulness of what has been delivered. The text adds that the measure must not be some form of earned value measure based on the delivery of documentation or the holding of meetings. Option B is the strongest distractor because counting finished items feels agile, but the guide measures the usefulness of the delivered solution to stakeholders, not the count of items.

question: A team plans to hold its only reflection session after the project closes. Which PM²-Agile principle does this break, and what does Appendix B.1 expect instead?

options.A: Sustainable development; the team should keep a constant pace indefinitely
options.B: Continuous attention on quality; the team should refactor after each release
options.C: Reflect at regular intervals; teams reflect at least at each iteration end
options.D: Simplicity; the team should maximise the amount of work that is not done

explanation: The principle is that at regular intervals the team reflects on how to improve, then tunes and adjusts its behaviour accordingly. Appendix B.1 says Agile teams reflect frequently, at least by the end of each iteration, and adopt techniques such as the **Iteration Retrospective** to generate insights and define concrete actions. Option B is the strongest distractor because quality is a real principle, but the guide's answer to a late-only reflection is the short feedback loop of principle 10, so that lessons learned are acted on regularly and not postponed indefinitely.

question: Appendix B of the PM²-Agile Guide contains a section numbered B.3. What does that section present?

options.A: The consolidated RASCI tables for the artefacts and the ceremonies
options.B: The PM² and PM²-Agile Artefacts Landscape, shown as one diagram
options.C: The full text of the twelve PM²-Agile Principles with commentary
options.D: The overview of PM²-Agile Activities & Artefacts across the phases

explanation: Section B.3 is titled **The PM² and PM²-Agile Artefacts Landscape** and shows the combined landscape as a single diagram; the same landscape appears earlier in the guide as Fig. 7.1. Option A is the strongest distractor, but the consolidated RASCI summary tables sit in section B.2, one page earlier. Option C is section B.1 and option D is section B.4.

question: In the summary table of Appendix B.2, which artefact is the only one listed under the Closing phase?

options.A: The Development Status Report
options.B: The Retrospectives Log
options.C: The Deployment Plan
options.D: The Project-End Report

explanation: The Closing block of the Appendix B.2 table contains a single row, the **Project-End Report**, where the Project Manager (PM) is Responsible and the Business Manager (BM) Supports. Options A and B are the strongest distractors because both are real PM²-Agile artefacts, but the table places them in the Executing block. The **Deployment Plan** appears in the Planning block.

question: In the Appendix B.2 table, exactly one row shows N/A in the Business Manager (BM) column. Which row is it?

options.A: The Iteration Retrospective meeting
options.B: The Iteration Planning meeting
options.C: The Daily Stand-up meeting
options.D: The Iteration Review meeting

explanation: The **Daily Stand-up** meeting row is the only one marked N/A for the Business Manager (BM); the rest of that row is PM Informed, TeCo Supports, PrOw Informed, ArOw Responsible and ATeM Responsible and Accountable. Option D is the strongest distractor, but the Business Manager is Consulted for the **Iteration Review** meeting, because that ceremony shows the working solution to the business. For the two other iteration ceremonies the Business Manager is Informed.

question: A Project Manager checks Appendix B.2 to see who is Responsible (R) for the Test Plan. What does the table show?

options.A: The Agile Team Member (ATeM) is R; the Project Manager (PM) is A
options.B: The Team Coordinator (TeCo) is R; the Project Manager (PM) is A
options.C: The Architecture Owner (ArOw) is R; the Team Coordinator is A
options.D: The Product Owner (PrOw) is R; the Business Manager (BM) is A

explanation: In the Planning block of the Appendix B.2 table the Test Plan row reads BM Informed, PM Accountable, TeCo Supports, PrOw Supports, ArOw Supports and ATeM Responsible. The Test Plan is the only Planning artefact where the **Agile Team Member (ATeM)** holds the R. Option B is the strongest distractor because the **Team Coordinator (TeCo)** is Responsible for most other Planning artefacts, such as the Development Handbook, the Development Work Plan, the Release Plan and the Deployment Plan.

question: What does the PM²-Agile Glossary say in its entry for Backlog?

options.A: It is the list of defects still open at the end of an iteration
options.B: It is the set of releases still waiting for deployment approval
options.C: Also known as Work Board; see the Iteration Plan for the detail
options.D: Also known as Product Backlog; see Work Items List (WIL)

explanation: The Glossary entry says Backlog is also known as Product Backlog and points the reader to the **Work Items List (WIL)**, which it names as the PM²-Agile term for Product Backlog. The separate entry for Product Backlog repeats that the equivalent in PM²-Agile is the Work Items List. Option C is the strongest distractor because the **Work Board** is a real Glossary term, but it is the physical or electronic board showing the state of Work Items in a current iteration, not the backlog itself.

question: The Glossary defines a Burndown Chart as work left to do versus time. Which item goes on which axis?

options.A: Completed work on the vertical axis, releases along the horizontal
options.B: Outstanding work on the vertical axis, time along the horizontal
options.C: Time on the vertical axis, outstanding work along the horizontal
options.D: Story points on the vertical axis, defect counts along the horizontal

explanation: The Glossary says the outstanding work, that is the **Work Items List**, is often on the vertical axis, with time along the horizontal. Option A is the strongest distractor because it describes the **Burnup Chart**, the neighbouring entry, which maps an upward trend of completed work until it reaches 100 percent. Option C simply swaps the two axes.

question: In the PM²-Agile Glossary entry for MoSCoW Prioritisation, what does the final W stand for?

options.A: Won't have this time, because the client rejected the item outright
options.B: Waiting for approval, pending the Appropriate Governance Body view
options.C: Want to have (but won't have this time), the lowest priority band
options.D: Work item to be split, because it is too large for one iteration

explanation: The Glossary spells **MoSCoW Prioritisation** as Must-have, Should-have, Could-have, and Want to have (but won't have this time). Option A is the strongest distractor because Won't have is the wording used in most other sources, so a candidate who relies on general agile knowledge will pick it. The PM²-Agile wording keeps the item as something the stakeholder wants, only not in this delivery.

question: A Team Coordinator (TeCo) reports the team's **Velocity**. Using the Glossary definition, what number is being reported?

options.A: The story points of stories finished over a timeboxed iteration
options.B: The hours of effort the team spent inside the timeboxed iteration
options.C: The number of work items still open at the end of the iteration
options.D: The percentage of the Work Items List completed since the release

explanation: The Glossary says the velocity of a team is the number of story points associated with stories that are finished over a timeboxed iteration. It counts finished work, and it counts it in story points, which the Glossary defines as a relative scale of effort. Option B is the strongest distractor because effort hours can also appear on an iteration burndown chart, but **Velocity** in PM²-Agile is measured in story points, not in hours.
